incidents.title: Vercel SPA 404 on Refresh & Git Push Rejection
incidents.inputState: React SPA deployed on Vercel threw a 404 error whenever refreshing non-root routes (e.g. /incidents).
incidents.failure:
Browser refresh returned Vercel 404 (Not Found).
git push was rejected (main -> main (fetch first)) when attempting to push the fix.
incidents.investigation:
Vercel checks disk for matching static files on refresh instead of handing routing over to index.html.
Remote main had new automated commits from GitHub Actions sync scripts that were missing locally.
incidents.rootCause:
Missing SPA rewrite rule in vercel.json.
Branch divergence between local and remote main.
incidents.resolution:
Added vercel.json with a rewrite rule (/(.*) -> /index.html).
Ran git pull --rebase origin main and pushed cleanly.
incidents.lessons:
SPAs on static hosting always need rewrite rules for client-side routing to survive page refreshes.
Use git pull --rebase on repos with active automated commit workflows.

incidents.title: Monolithic Client Bundle Bloat & Route-Tree Starvation (1.88 MB Initial Payload)
incidents.inputState: Storefront player/developer clicking a game card from /store navigating to /store/games/:id.
incidents.failure:
React ErrorBoundary triggered with full-screen crash:

[GameStation ErrorBoundary Caught] ReferenceError: Terminal is not defined at GameDetails (GameDetails.tsx:193:16)
incidents.investigation: Inspected `Frontend/src/Pages/Storefront/GameDetails.tsx` at line 193. The component attempted to render `<Terminal className="..." />` inside the system requirements HUD, but the `Terminal` icon was missing from the `lucide-react` import list. Concurrently, uncertified games in `PENDING` review returned `404 Not Found` to developers attempting preview.
incidents.rootCause:
1. Unused import cleanup inadvertently stripped `Terminal` from `lucide-react` imports in `GameDetails.tsx`.
2. Backend `/api/store/games/:id` strictly filtered by `status: 'PUBLISHED'`, preventing studio developers from previewing their own pending submissions.
incidents.resolution:
1. Restored `Terminal` to the `lucide-react` import statement in `GameDetails.tsx`.
2. Attached `optionalToken` middleware to `Backend/src/Routes/store.routes.ts` and updated `getStoreGameById` to allow creators, admins, and owners to view games in `PENDING` certification.
incidents.lessons:
1. Run `tsc -b` and end-to-end route smoke tests before pushing UI component changes.
2. Error boundaries prevent platform-wide blank screens, but route-level unit checks must validate optional icon dependencies and preview authorization logic.

incidents.title: GameStation Trailer Video Playback
incidents.inputState: Navigating to the game details page (/store/games/:id) where the media gallery was expected to automatically play the developer's submitted YouTube trailer URL.
incidents.failure: The video viewport showed a dead black box displaying static text VIDEO PLAYER INITIALIZING... [URL] with no actual playback and no clickable link
incidents.investigation: Inspected MediaGallery.tsx and found a hardcoded placeholder <div> printing raw text instead of mounting player engine.
incidents.rootCause: The component was an unfinished mock stub, and web browsers cannot natively play YouTube URLs inside HTML5 <video> tags without embedding YouTube's player API.
incidents.resolution: Added regex to extract the 11-char YouTube ID, embedded a privacy-friendly youtube-nocookie.com iframe with autoplay=1&mute=1, and added native <video> fallback for raw .mp4 uploads.
incidents.lessons: Never leave placeholder mock UI in production customer flows, and always pair web video autoplay with muted to prevent modern browsers from blocking playback.

incidents.title: Template Frontmatter Ignored by GitHub Issue Parser
incidents.inputState: The portfolio's incident logging system relies on a standardized GitHub Issue Template (.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/engineering-incident.md). This template pre-fills the issue description with the required markdown headers (## INPUT_STATE, ## FAILURE, etc.) and automatically applies the engineering-incident label via YAML frontmatter.
incidents.failure:
When creating a new issue, GitHub did not recognize the file as an Issue Template. Instead of presenting a template selector, it routed to a blank issue page. Furthermore, the YAML configuration block was rendered as plain text inside the issue body, and the engineering-incident label was not automatically applied. 
Because the label was missing, the ETL pipeline fetched 0 incidents.
incidents.investigation:
Inspected the markdown syntax of the .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/engineering-incident.md file. 
The YAML configuration block was formatted as:
name: Engineering Incident
description: ...
However, a standard YAML frontmatter block strictly requires three dashes (---) at both the beginning and the end of the block.
incidents.rootCause: The template file was missing the opening --- at Line 1. Without this standard YAML delimiter, the GitHub backend parser failed to recognize the configuration block, gracefully degrading the file to a standard markdown document and ignoring all automated labeling and title instructions.
incidents.resolution:
Added the missing --- to the first line of the file and changed the description key to the correct GitHub keyword about. 
Once pushed to the repository, the GitHub UI successfully parsed the template, presented the template selector to the user, and automatically applied the engineering-incident label upon issue creation.
incidents.lessons: Strict parsers (like YAML frontmatter parsers) have zero tolerance for syntax deviations. When building automation pipelines that rely on strict file structures, always validate the syntax locally or check the vendor documentation for exact formatting requirements before pushing to production.

incidents.title: GitHub Actions 403 Forbidden on Automated Commits
incidents.inputState: The portfolio uses a scheduled ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) pipeline via GitHub Actions. A Node.js script fetches live project metrics, DSA stats, and incident logs, and the Action attempts to commit and push the updated JSON data back to the repository.
incidents.failure:
The GitHub Action workflow failed during the git push step. 
The terminal logs displayed a fatal error: remote: Permission to martand-codes/Portfolio.git denied to github-actions[bot]. fatal: unable to access ... 403. 
The automated data pipeline was completely broken, preventing live data from reaching the production UI.
incidents.investigation:
Verified that the GITHUB_TOKEN secret was being correctly passed into the workflow environment. 
Checked the repository settings and realized that the default GitHub Actions token scope only granted read-only permissions to the repository contents. 
The script successfully pulled the data and modified incidents-data.json locally on the runner, but the bot was unauthorized to push those file modifications back to the main branch.
incidents.rootCause: By default, GitHub repository settings restrict the github-actions[bot] permissions to "Read-only" for security purposes. The workflow required "Read and write permissions" to execute git commit and git push.
incidents.resolution:
Navigated to the repository Settings -> Actions -> General.
Changed the "Workflow permissions" setting from "Read repository contents and packages permissions" to "Read and write permissions". 
Triggered the workflow manually, and the data files were successfully committed and pushed to the repository.
incidents.lessons: When designing automated GitOps pipelines where a CI/CD runner modifies and pushes code, always verify the token scope. The default security posture for CI runners is typically read-only, and write permissions must be explicitly granted and audited.

incidents.title: Differential Upgrade 400 Bad Request & Checkout Concurrency Anomalies
incidents.inputState: User with an owned game edition attempted to view and upgrade editions on `/store/games/:id`. System was expected to recognize the highest owned tier and disable duplicate purchases.
incidents.failure: Clicking "Upgrade Edition" triggered a 400 Bad Request: Simultaneously, concurrent requests for free claims threw `P2002 Unique constraint failed on (userId, gameId)` (500 error), and parallel checkout requests generated duplicate payable Stripe sessions.
incidents.investigation:
1. Queried database: User had 2 payments:
   - Base Deluxe Edition: `amount = ₹79.99`
   - Ultimate Upgrade: `amount = ₹20.00`, `pricing.price = ₹99.99`
2. `checkGameOwnership` queried `Payment` with `orderBy: { amount: "desc" }`.
3. Because the upgrade was a differential fee (`₹20.00 < ₹79.99`), the query selected the base tier instead of the upgraded tier.
4. Stress-tested with 10 concurrent requests via a test script to identify race condition bottlenecks.
incidents.rootCause:
**Missing Checkout Idempotency:** Concurrent checkout requests created duplicate Stripe sessions due to lack of idempotency keys.
**Non-Idempotent Free Claims:** Free game path used `prisma.create()` instead of `upsert()`, causing unhandled unique-constraint crashes under parallel load.
incidents.resolution:
1. **Corrected Tier Evaluation:** Refactored `checkGameOwnership` and `createCheckoutSession` to determine ownership ceiling via `pricing.price` across all successful payments.
2. **Stripe Idempotency & Session Reuse:**
   - Added deterministic Stripe `idempotencyKey` headers (`cs-single-${userId}-${gameId}-${pricingId}-${timeBucket}`).
   - Added reuse of open `PENDING` sessions within a 30-minute window.
   - Used `prisma.payment.upsert()` on `@unique providerSessionId`.
3. **Atomic Entitlements:** Replaced `prisma.userLibrary.create()` with `prisma.userLibrary.upsert()`.
incidents.lessons:
- Financial transaction amounts cannot represent entitlement tiers in differential pricing architectures.
- External API calls (payment gateways) require upstream idempotency keys; database constraints alone cannot prevent double-charging.
- Any write to a table with unique constraints must be idempotent (`upsert`) to guarantee concurrency safety.

incidents.title: Prisma Upgrade Broke the Database Toolchain
incidents.inputState:
GameStation was being developed with TypeScript, Node.js,
PostgreSQL and Prisma as the ORM/database layer.

The project was upgraded to a newer Prisma version while the
database schema and existing application code were already in use.
incidents.failure:
The Prisma upgrade introduced compatibility and initialization
problems across the existing database setup.

The project began producing Prisma-related errors that prevented
the normal development workflow from functioning correctly.

The issue became particularly difficult because the failure was not
isolated to a single application query; the ORM/client setup itself
was affected.
incidents.investigation:
Inspected the Prisma schema, generated client, package versions and
database configuration.

The dependency versions were compared against the existing project
setup and the behavior of the newly generated Prisma client.

The investigation showed that the newer Prisma version introduced
changes incompatible with the project's existing configuration and
usage.
incidents.rootCause:
The project had moved to a newer Prisma release whose behavior and
client/tooling requirements were not compatible with the existing
GameStation database setup.

The dependency upgrade was therefore treated as a breaking change
rather than a routine package update.
incidents.resolution:
Rolled Prisma back to the previously compatible version and
regenerated the Prisma client.

The database workflow was then restored and development could
continue using the stable Prisma configuration.
incidents.lessons:
ORM upgrades are not automatically safe just because the application
code itself has not changed.

Before upgrading a core infrastructure dependency, verify:

- version compatibility
- generated client behavior
- database adapter/configuration requirements
- migration behavior
- existing application integration

A working dependency version should be treated as part of the
project's infrastructure contract.

incidents.title: Authentication Failure During Production Login
incidents.inputState:
Aankhodekha's authentication system was deployed as part of the
production backend.
incidents.failure:
Login requests resulted in HTTP 500 errors.

The backend logs contained:

passlib.exc.UnknownHashError

The authentication endpoint was therefore unable to correctly process
the stored password hash.
incidents.investigation:
Inspected the backend logs and traced the failure through the
authentication/password verification path.

The error originated from the password hashing/verification layer
rather than from the HTTP routing layer itself.
incidents.rootCause:
The authentication system encountered a password hash that the
configured password hashing implementation could not correctly
interpret.
incidents.resolution:
Corrected the password hashing/authentication configuration and
verified the login flow again after deployment.
incidents.lessons:
Authentication failures should be investigated from the complete
request path:

HTTP request → authentication route → password verification →
stored credential format.

A successful deployment does not guarantee that existing authentication
data is compatible with the runtime configuration.

incidents.title: Docker Bloat
incidents.inputState: Aankhodekha's containerized system was being packaged with the complete inference environment, including CUDA/ML dependencies.
incidents.failure:
Docker storage consumption became disproportionately large.

The backend image reached approximately 11.6 GB and Docker reported a
large amount of reclaimable storage.

The storage pressure eventually consumed the available space on the
local C: drive reaching 0 bytes free.
incidents.investigation:
Inspected Docker image, container, volume, and build cache usage using
Docker's disk usage tooling.

Reviewed the available storage on the C: drive and investigated which
Docker artifacts were consuming the space.

The investigation showed that the ML/CUDA environment contributed
substantially to the container footprint.
incidents.rootCause:
The Aankhodekha backend required heavyweight ML/GPU runtime dependencies
for inference, resulting in a substantially larger container footprint
than a conventional API service.

Repeated Docker image rebuilds also accumulated storage through images,
layer, and build cache.
incidents.resolution:
Reclaimed Docker storage by removing unnecessary images, containers,
and build-cache data.

The available disk space was restored and the deployment environment
was able to continue operating.
incidents.lessons:
Avoid rebuilding the complete Docker Compose stack unnecessarily for
small application changes.

Understand Docker's image layers and build cache before repeatedly
rebuilding large ML-based images, and monitor Docker disk usage when
working with heavyweight inference environments.

incidents.title: Camera Ingestion
incidents.inputState:
Aankhodekha was processing multiple camera feeds concurrently.
The ANPR pipeline used YOLO for vehicle/plate detection and
PaddleOCR for plate recognition.
incidents.failure:
Concurrent ingestion caused PaddleOCR/native runtime failures,
including SIGSEGV and memory corruption errors such as:

malloc(): unsorted double linked list corrupted and backend completely fell apart
incidents.investigation:
The failure appeared specifically under concurrent processing. It was too slow and it froze the terminal
Sequential ingestion was tested first and completed successfully.
incidents.rootCause:
Concurrent execution of the OCR/inference path was identified as
the primary suspect.

The crash occurred at the native process level, meaning a normal
Python try/except could not reliably recover from the failure.
incidents.resolution:
Changed the ingestion strategy to sequential processing.

The complete camera set was then processed successfully, producing
44 persisted events across the available camera videos.
incidents.lessons:
Native crashes require a different debugging strategy from ordinary
Python exceptions.

Before adding more error handling, reproduce the failure,
identify the execution path, and isolate the concurrency boundary.
